title: N-Terminal Protein Sequencing by Nicotinic Acid Derivatization and MS Analysis
projectDescription: Most MS-based workflows for N-terminal protein sequence analysis rely on the modification of primary amines at the protein N-terminus and lysine residues, in many cases through dimethylation. However, incomplete dimethyl labeling and undesired side reactions have been reported previously and were also observed in our experiments. In this study, we evaluated alternative methods for N-terminal protein derivatization. For reductive methylation, the highly toxic reducing agent sodium cyanoborohydride was successfully replaced by pyridine borane. In addition, several single-reagent labeling approaches were applied to model proteins and compared to the dimethylation workflow. Criteria for the selection of suitable reagents were completeness and selectivity of the protein derivatization reaction, the detection sensitivity for modified peptides by mass spectrometry, and the absence of undesirable side reactions. Comparative analyses demonstrated that the chemical derivatization of free amines by nicotinic acid N-hydroxysuccinimide ester is a particularly promising approach for N-terminal protein sequencing. Protocols for the nicotinoylation of proteins in solution or in gel using this reagent were optimized and successfully applied to various test proteins.
dataProcessingProtocol: MS and MS/MS spectra were converted to Mascot generic format (MGF) files by using Proteome Discoverer, version 2.1 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The MGF files were searched against the UniProtKB bovine protein (taxonomy: 9913, 32405 sequences), horse protein (taxonomy: 9796, 28093 sequences), or E. coli protein database (taxonomy: 83334, 5568 sequences). The Mascot search engine (Matrix Science, London, UK; version 3.0.0) was used for peptide and protein sequence identification [35]. Mascot searches were performed with a parent ion mass tolerance of 7 ppm and a fragment ion mass tolerance of 10 ppm. Typically, a target false discovery rate of 1 % was selected, and the results were refined with machine learning using Percolator. Enzyme specificity was set to semi-specific trypsin, allowing up to three missed cleavages, or semi-specific chymotrypsin, allowing up to four missed cleavages. Cleavages at phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, leucine, and methionine were considered as specific for purified chymotrypsin (Roche), and cleavages at phenylalanine, tyrosine, and leucine as specific for recombinant chymotrypsin (Promega). Oxidation of methionine, N-terminal acetylation of proteins, and the chemical modifications of interest were specified as variable modifications on N-terminal amino acids and on lysine residues. The chemical modifications included mono- and dimethylation, nicotinoylation (mass increase of 105.0215 Da), and reaction products with RapiFluor (+ 312.1586 Da), 2-PCA (+ 89.0265 Da or + 107.0311 Da), and TMTduplex (+ 225.1558 Da) reagents. For the detection of side reactions of TMT and nicotinic acid NHS ester reagents, serine, threonine, and tyrosine were considered as potential acceptor sites. The following side reaction products of amino groups induced by the treatment with formaldehyde and sodium cyanoborohydride were included as variable modifications: Methylol (+ 30.0106 Da), methylol and methylation, cyanomethylation (+ 39.0109 Da), cyanomethylation and methylation, N-terminal cyclization product (N-methyl-4-imidazolidinone, + 12.0000 Da) without and with additional methylation.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Dimethylation. 25 µg of protein in HEPES buffer (pH 7.5) were dimethylated in formaldehyde(50 mM) and sodium cyanoborohydride (25 mM) or pyridine borane (50 mM) for 2 h at RT. Pyridine borane was diluted 1:8 with ethanol and added to the aqueous reaction solution, resulting in a final ethanol concentration of 5% (v/v). In the optimized protocol, TCEP was added to a concentration of 4 mM, and guanidine HCl to a concentration of 4 M. RapiFluor derivatization. 15 - 40 μg of protein in 30 µl of phosphate buffer (pH 6.5) werelabeled using RapiFluor in reagent to protein ratios of 20:1 or 60:1 at RT for 30 min.  2-PCA derivatization. 25 µg of protein in HEPES buffer (pH 7.5) were incubated with 20 mM 2-PCA and 5 mM TCEP for 3 h at 37°C.   TMTduplex labeling: 25 μg of protein in 45 ul of 50 mM TEAB solution (pH 8.5) were labeled with 100 ug TMT2-126 or TMT2-127 reagent dissolved in 15 ul acetonitrile during 1 h at room temperature. Nicotinic acid modification. Proteins were dissolved in HEPES buffer pH 7.5 (100 mM final concentration) containing 4 mM TCEP and 4 M guanidine hydrochloride. A solution of 100 mM nicotinic acid NHS ester in 65% ethanol was added to a concentration of 20 mM in the sample solution, and the reaction time at RT was 2 h. To quench the reagent, 1% of hydroxylamine was added, the pH was increased to 10 by the addition of 1% ammonium hydroxide, and the reaction was allowed to proceed for 1 h at RT.   Nicotinic acid NHS ester derivatization of proteins in gel. Proteins were separated in NuPAGE 4 - 12% Bis-Tris gels (1mm; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Gel bands were excised, washed twice with, and dried. The nicotinoylation reaction was conducted in 100 mM HEPES buffer (pH 7.5) containing 4 mM TCEP. A 200 mM stock solution of nicotinic acid NHS ester in 65% of ethanol was added to a final concentration of 40 mM reagent, The reaction was allowed toproceed for 2 h at room temperature (25°C). The reagent was inactivated by the addition ofhydroxylamine. Proteolytic digestion of proteins in solution   Proteins labeled with RapiFluor or TMT reagents were proteolytically digested by using theFASP method. All other protein samples were cleaved by using the SP3 protocol. Carboxylate-modified magnetic beads were washed with water. Ethanol was added to a final volume of 70-80%. SP3 beads were mixed with proteins in a 1:10 ratio (w/w) protein/beads. 2% of trypsin or 2 - 4% of chymotrypsin were added, and the proteolytic digestion on SP3 beads was conducted in TEAB solution overnight, typically at RT.    LC-MS/MS analysis   DDA analyses were performed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid MS or on a Q Exactive Orbitrap MS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Both instruments were coupled to an AQUITY UPLC M-class system (Waters). Liquid chromatography solvent compositions of buffers A and B were 0.1% formic acid in water and 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile, respectively. Sample solutions were loaded onto a Symmetry C18 trap column (100 Å, 5 µm, 180 µm x 20 mm, Waters) and separated on a HSS T3 analytical column (100 Å, 1.8 µm, 75 µm x 250 mm, Waters). Peptides were eluted at a flow rate of 300 nL/min.   For the Orbitrap Lumos analyses, the following LC gradient was applied: 0 - 3 min: 5% buffer B, 43 min: 25% B, 53 min: 60% B, 63 min: 95% B. Survey scans were acquired in the Orbitrap mass analyzer in the range of m/z 300 - 2000, with a resolution of 120000, an automated gain control (AGC) target value of 400000, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms.HCD spectra were acquired in the Orbitrap mass analyzer, using a normalized collision energy of 33%, a resolution of 60000, an AGC target value of 50000, and a maximum injection time of 118 ms. Precursor ions were isolated in the quadrupole with an m/z 1.6 isolation window. Charge state screening was enabled, and the threshold value for signal intensities was 25000. Precursor ion masses already selected for MS/MS acquisition were excluded for 30 s.   The following LC gradient was used for the Q Exactive Orbitrap analyses: 0 - 3 min: 3% buffer B, 45 min: 35% B, 50 min: 60% B, 60 min: 95% B. Survey scans were acquired in the range of m/z 300-1500, with a resolution of 70000, an automated gain control (AGC) target value of 3000000, and a maximum injection time of 100 ms. HCD spectra were acquired by using normalized collision energy of 25%, a resolution of 35000, an AGC target value of 100000, and a maximum injection time of 120 ms. Precursor ions were isolated in the quadrupole with an m/z 1.6 isolation window. Precursor ions with charge state 1 or unassigned charge states were excluded. The 12 most intense precursor ions were selected for MS/MS acquisition. The threshold value for signal intensities was 25000. Precursor ion masses already selected for MS/MS acquisition were excluded for 10 s.

title: A unified HILIC-FLD-MS workflow for simultaneous peptide and released N-glycan mapping of protein biopharmaceuticals
projectDescription: The study explored peptide mapping and released/RFMS-labeled N-glycan profiling in a single HILIC-FLD-MS chromatographic run as an alternative to separate peptide RPLC-MS mapping and HILIC-FLD assay of labeled glycans. Individual LC data files are annotated in the DataDescription.xlsx file.
dataProcessingProtocol: MS spectra were searched in Byonic v3.5.0 against the individual FASTA sequences of biopharmaceuticals or a 5-protein combined library, all appended with common contaminants. The mass tolerance was 10 ppm for precursors and 18 ppm for fragments. A fully or semispecific cleavage with two missed cleavages was used. Oxidized Met, deamidated Asn, ammonia loss from Asn, pyroGlu formation from N-terminal Glu and Gln, and dehydrated Asp were set as dynamic modifications. The search space included a built-in Byonic library of 164 mammalian N-glycan compositions uploaded to the repository as .XLSX files. Carbamidomethylation of Cys was set as a static modification. Peptide-spectrum matches identified with a 2D FDR ≤ 1%  were considered.  The spectra assigned to fully tryptic peptides were processed in Skyline, considering three monoisotopic peaks and precursor charge states ranging from 1+ to 6+.  Annotation of labeled glycans was performed in Skyline using targeted MS1 filtering based on the Byonic library described above, with precursor m/z values adjusted for RFMS labeling. Spectra were filtered with a 5 ppm mass tolerance, charge states 1+ to 3+, and extraction of three monoisotopic peaks. Glycans with similar precursor masses were distinguished using Neu5Ac+ oxonium fragments to identify sialylated species, and Y1/Y2 ions corresponding to RFMS-GlcNAc1/2+ ± Fuc to confirm core fucosylation. Additional criteria included expected retention times and elution order reported in the literature, as well as consistency with known biosynthetic pathways.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Aqueous stock solutions of the selected seven iRT peptides (LFLQFGAQGSPFLK, GTFIIDPGGVIR, YILAGVENSK, TPVITGAPYEYR, DGLDAASYYAPVR, ADVTPADFSEWSK, and VEATFGVDESNAK) were enriched with 0.001% PEG 20 000 and mixed to achieve similar concentrations of around 25 ng/μL.  Reconstituted therapeutic proteins were desalted and denatured at 2 µg/µL in 0.5% RapiGest SF prepared in 75 mM HEPES, pH 7.5, by incubation at 90 °C for 3 min. N-deglycosylation was performed using Rapid PNGase F at 50 °C for 5 min according to the manufacturer’s instructions, with 1.2 µL of enzyme stock added per 40 µg of protein. Released N-glycans were labeled using RapiFluor-MS labeling reagent at a final concentration of 20 μg/μL in 25% dimethyl formamide for 5 min at room temperature. The reaction mixture (40 µL) was diluted to 400 µL with acetonitrile (ACN) and loaded onto an in-house-prepared microSPE column packed with 5 mg of Spe-ed NH₂ aminopropyl sorbent in a Pierce Micro-Spin cartridge. The microSPE column was conditioned with water and equilibrated with 85% ACN, using 200 µL of each. After sample loading, glycans were washed with 1200 µL of 1% FA in 90% ACN and eluted with 90 µL of 200 mM ammonium acetate, pH 7, in 5% ACN. The SPE recovery was approximately 60%.  Reconstituted therapeutic proteins were denatured and reduced in 5 M guanidine hydrochloride containing 20 mM dithiothreitol at 37 °C for 30 min. Free thiol groups were blocked with 25 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min at room temperature in the dark. Proteins were subsequently desalted using Zeba spin columns and digested overnight at 37 °C with dimethylated SOLu-trypsin in 25% Low-Artifact Digestion Buffer at an enzyme-to-protein mass ratio of 1:50. Digestion was quenched by the addition of difluoroacetic acid, and the resulting digest was supplemented with 0.001% PEG 20 000.  For the LC-MS-related method description and treatment of prepared samples, see the manuscript.

title: An Atlas of Human Glycosylation Pathways Enables Display of the Human Glycome by Gene Engineered Cells
projectDescription: The structural diversity of glycans on cells – the glycome – is vast and complex to decipher. Glycan arrays have played a pivotal role in exploring the informational content of glycans. Current glycan arrays display oligosaccharides generated by chemical and chemoenzymatic synthesis or isolated from biological sources and are used to report glycan hapten binding epitopes. Glycan arrays are limited resources, produced through considerable efforts, and they display individual saccharides without the natural context of other glycans and glycoconjugates at the cell surface. We usedmaps of glycosylation pathways to generate a library of isogenic HEK293 cells with combinatorially engineered glycosylation capacities designed to display and dissect the genetic, biosynthetic and structural basis for glycan binding epitopes in a natural context. This expandable and self-renewable cell-based glycan array reports glycosyltransferase genes required (or blocking) for interactions through logic sequential biosynthetic steps, which not only predicts essential structural features of involved glycans including the glycoconjugate context, but importantly provides instructions for enzymatic synthesis, recombinant production, and genetic strategies to dissect biological functions. The broad utility of this cell-based glycan array and its comprehensive read-out is demonstrated by dissecting glycan-binding specificities of microbial adhesins, and the discovery power is demonstrated by uncovering higher order binding of microbial adhesins to clustered patches of O-glycans organized by their presentation on proteins.
dataProcessingProtocol: Mass Spectrometry LC MS/MS analysis was performed on EASY-nLC 1200 UHPLC (Thermo Scientific) interfaced via nanoSpray Flex ion source to an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos MS (Thermo Scientific). Briefly, the nLC was operated in a single analytical column set up using PicoFrit Emitters (New Objectives, 75 μm inner diameter) packed in-house with Reprosil-Pure-AQ C18 phase (Dr. Maisch, 1.9-μm particle size, 19-21 cm column length). Each sample was injected onto the column and eluted in gradients from 3 to 32 % B for glycopeptides, and 10 to 40% for released and labeled glycans in 45 min at 200 nL/min (Solvent A, 100% H2O; Solvent B, 80% acetonitrile; both containing 0.1 % (v/v) formic acid). A precursor MS1 scan (m/z 350–2,000) of intact peptides was acquired in the Orbitrap at the nominal resolution setting of 120,000, followed by Orbitrap HCD-MS2 and at the nominal resolution setting of 60,000 of the five most abundant multiply charged precursors in the MS1 spectrum; a minimum MS1 signal threshold of 50,000 was used for triggering data-dependent fragmentation events. Targeted MS/MS analysis was performed by setting up a targeted MSn (tMSn) Scan Properties pane. A target list was composed from top 30 most abundant glycans or glycopeptides from the proposed compositional list Data Analysis Glycan and glycopeptide compositional analysis was performed from m/z features extracted from LC-MS data using in-house written SysBioWare software (Vakhrushev et al., 2009). For m/z feature recognition from full MS scans LFQ Profiler Node of the Proteome discoverer 2.2 (Thermo Scientific) was used. The list of precursor ions (m/z, charge, peak area) was imported as ASCII data into SysBioWare and compositional assignment within 3 ppm mass tolerance was performed. The main building blocks used for the compositional analysis were: NeuAc, Hex, HexNAc, dHex and the theoretical mass increment of the most prominent peptide corresponding to each potential glycosites. The most prominent peptide sequence related to N-glycosite of interest was determined experimentally by comparing the yield of deamidated peptides before and after PNGase F treatment. One or two phosphate groups were added as building blocks for assignment. To generation the potential glycopeptide list, all the glycoforms with an abundance higher than 10% of the most abundant glycoform were used for glycan feature analysis. All high mannose and hybrid structures were excluded in the TCL data.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Production of N- and O-glycosylation reporter proteins A reporter for N-glycosylation was designed as a secreted construct of the FcgRIIa N-glycoprotein, encoding the extracellular domain (aa1-217, UniproP12318) fused with a 10xHis tag. Secreted FcgRIIa was transiently produced in suspension HEK293-6E cells. Briefly, 30 ml of HEK293-6E cells were seeded at a cell density of 0.5 × 106 cells/ml and transfected the next day with 30 μg of the secrete FcgRIIa construct and 90 μg of PEI (1:3 ratio) incubated at room temp. for 15 min and cultured for 72 h before harvest. A reporter for GalNAc-type O-glycosylation was designed as a secreted construct of the mucin MUC1 encoding TRs (also used for the mucin display). The reporter was stable expressed in HEK293-6E after G418 selection, and a stable pool of cells were seed at a cell density of 1.0 x 106 cells/ml and cultured 72 h. Secreted FcgRIIa and MUC1 were purified from culture medium by nickel affinity chromatography. Media was mixed 3:1 (v/v) in 4× binding buffer (100 mM sodium phosphate, pH 7.4, 2 M NaCl) and applied to self-packed nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) affinity resin column (Qiagen), pre-equilibrated in washing buffer (25 mM sodium phosphate, pH 7.4, 500 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole). After washing, bound protein was eluted with 200 mM imidazole in washing buffer. The protein containing fractions were identified by SDS-PAGE, and further purified by reverse-phase HPLC with a Jupiter 5 μ C4 300A column (Phenomenex, Torrence, CA), using 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and a gradient of 10–100% acetonitrile. Sample preparation for site-specific N-glycopeptide analysis 20 μg of the purified FcgRIIa were dissolved in 50mM ammonium bicarbonate (AmBic) buffer, reduced in 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) at 60°C for 45 min), alkylated (20 mM iodoacetamide (IAA), in dark at RT for 30 min), reduced again (10 mM DTT, 20°C, RT) and digested with 0,8U chymotrypsin (1:25 ratio chymotrypsin:protein) (Roche) (25°C, 4h). The proteolytic digest was desalted by in-house produced modified StageTip columns containing 3 layers of C18 membrane (3M Empore disks from Sigma Aldrich) (Rappsilber et al., 2007). Samples were eluted with 50% methanol in 0.1% formic acid (FA), dried in SpeedVac and re-solubilized in 0.1% FA and submitted for LC MS/MS analysis. Sample preparation for total cell lysate N-glycan analysis The packed cell pellets (1x107 cells) were lysed in 1 mg Rapigest SF Surfactant (Waters), 50 mM AmBic and homogenized by sonication. Cleared lysates were heated (95°C, 15 min), diluted in 50 mM AmBic to a final concentration of 0.2% Rapigest and sonicated again followed by reduction (10 mM DTT, 60°C, 45 min), alkylation (20 mM iodoacetamide, in dark at RT for 30 min), reduction (10 mM DTT, RT, 20 min) and digested with 25U trypsin (Roche) in 50mM AmBic (37°C, 12 h, 650 rpm). Each tryptic digest was acidified with TFA and incubated at 37°C for 30 min before centrifuging (max speed, RT, 15 min). Sep- Pak C18 columns (Waters) where washed with 100% methanol, 50% methanol 0.1% FA and equilibrated with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) before loading the supernatants containing the tryptic digests. After reloading the flow through, the column was washed with 0.1% TFA, twice with 0.1% FA and eluted twice with 50% methanol 0.1% FA. Freeze-dried samples were resuspended in 50 mM AmBic with 8U PNGaseF (Roche) and incubated at 37°C for 16 h. The digest was applied to Sep-pak C18 column, as described above, and flow through containing the released N-glycans was collected for further labeling with Rapifluor-MS glycan kit (Waters) as described by manufacturers.  Sample preparation for O-glycopeptide analysis Approximately 50 μg of the purified MUC1 reporter was reduced, alkylated and digested with 10 μg endo-AspN (Roche) (37°C, O/N). The digested sample was fractionated by C18 HPLC, and the MUC1 20mer TR glycopeptide identified and analyzed by LC-MS/MS.
